mls-u1-concept-01.title: The ML attack surface
mls-u1-concept-01.body: An ML system is a pipeline, and every stage can be attacked: data collection, labelling, training, the stored model, the serving API, and whatever consumes the output. A sound model can still be compromised through its training data or through the script that loads it.
mls-u1-concept-01.example: A spam filter is retrained every week on messages that users report.
exampleSteps: Data stage: anyone who can send mail and report it influences the training set.
Serving stage: a sender can probe which wording gets through.
Output stage: the mail client acts automatically on the verdict.
mls-u1-concept-01.takeaway: Model the whole pipeline, not only the trained model.

mls-u1-concept-02.title: Security goals for models
mls-u1-concept-02.body: The classic goals translate directly. Integrity means the model behaves as intended, availability means it keeps serving useful results, and confidentiality covers both the model itself and the data it learned from. Generative systems add misuse, where the model is turned to producing harmful output.
mls-u1-concept-02.example: A medical imaging model is deployed in a hospital.
exampleSteps: Integrity failure: a crafted scan is classified as healthy.
Availability failure: poisoned retraining makes every prediction unusable.
Confidentiality failure: an attacker learns that a patient was in the training set.
mls-u1-concept-02.takeaway: Name the goal being violated before you choose a defence.

mls-u1-concept-03.title: Adversaries are not noise
mls-u1-concept-03.body: Ordinary reliability work asks how a model performs on average over natural inputs. Security asks how it performs on the worst input an adaptive attacker can find. A model can be excellent on the first measure and fail completely on the second.
mls-u1-concept-03.example: A vision model is tested against blur, rain and low light.
exampleSteps: It stays accurate because those shifts are random and do not aim at its weaknesses.
An attacker instead searches for the one small change that flips its output.
mls-u1-concept-03.takeaway: A held-out test set measures average behaviour. It says little about a motivated attacker.

mls-u1-concept-04.title: Why ML bugs resist patching
mls-u1-concept-04.body: A conventional vulnerability is usually a specific flaw with a specific fix. An ML weakness is often spread across millions of learned parameters, so there is no faulty line to change. Fixes tend to be statistical: they reduce how often an attack works without removing the class of attack.
mls-u1-concept-04.example: A filter misses one phrasing of a banned request.
exampleSteps: Adding that phrasing to the training data fixes that phrasing.
A slightly reworded version may still pass, so the weakness has narrowed rather than closed.
mls-u1-concept-04.takeaway: Expect mitigation and monitoring for ML weaknesses, not a one-time patch.

mls-u1-concept-05.title: Attacker goals
mls-u1-concept-05.body: An untargeted attacker wants any wrong output. A targeted attacker wants one specific wrong output. Targeted attacks are harder, but they are often the ones that pay off, because the attacker usually has a particular outcome in mind.
mls-u1-concept-05.example: A traffic sign classifier reads a stop sign.
exampleSteps: Untargeted: any label other than stop counts as success.
Targeted: the model must say speed limit 60.
mls-u1-concept-05.takeaway: Always state which outcome counts as success for the attacker.

mls-u1-concept-06.title: Attacker knowledge
mls-u1-concept-06.body: White-box attackers know the architecture and weights. Black-box attackers can only query the system and see its outputs. Grey-box attackers sit between, perhaps knowing the training data or model family but not the weights. Less knowledge usually means more queries or lower success, not safety.
mls-u1-concept-06.example: Three attackers target a licensed face-matching model.
exampleSteps: A former employee with the weights is white-box.
A competitor who knows it is a public ResNet tuned on private data is grey-box.
A stranger using the public API is black-box.
mls-u1-concept-06.takeaway: Knowledge sets the attack’s cost. It does not decide whether an attack exists.

mls-u1-concept-07.title: Attacker capabilities
mls-u1-concept-07.body: Capability describes what the attacker can touch. Common cases are control of inputs at inference, control of some training data or labels, control of the model itself, and query access to the API. Capabilities decide which attack classes are even possible.
mls-u1-concept-07.example: A public image API accepts uploads but never retrains on them.
exampleSteps: Users control inference inputs and have query access.
They have no training data control, so poisoning through that API is ruled out.
mls-u1-concept-07.takeaway: List what the attacker can actually reach, then rule out what they cannot.

mls-u1-concept-08.title: Secrecy is not a defence
mls-u1-concept-08.body: Kerckhoffs’s principle says a system should stay secure even if everything except the key is public. Hidden architectures and private weights raise an attacker’s cost, but surrogates, leaks and transfer attacks wear that advantage down. Treat secrecy as friction, never as the security boundary.
mls-u1-concept-08.example: A vendor argues that nobody can attack its detector because its features are proprietary.
exampleSteps: An attacker trains a surrogate on public data.
Examples crafted against the surrogate often transfer to the real detector.
mls-u1-concept-08.takeaway: Assume the attacker eventually learns how your model works.

mls-u1-concept-09.title: The NIST taxonomy
mls-u1-concept-09.body: NIST AI 100-2 organises adversarial ML by the type of system, predictive or generative, and by attacker goal, knowledge and capability. For predictive AI, the main classes are evasion at inference, poisoning at training, and privacy attacks. It gives teams common vocabulary.
mls-u1-concept-09.example: A team writes up three incidents.
exampleSteps: Crafted inputs fooling a deployed classifier are evasion.
Tampered training records are poisoning.
Recovering details of training records is a privacy attack.
mls-u1-concept-09.takeaway: Use shared terms so that reports and defences can be compared.

mls-u1-concept-10.title: MITRE ATLAS
mls-u1-concept-10.body: ATLAS is a knowledge base of adversary tactics and techniques against AI systems, modelled on ATT&CK and supported by case studies. Tactics describe why a step is taken and techniques describe how. It helps teams plan red-team exercises and map detections to real behaviour.
mls-u1-concept-10.example: An incident report lists several steps.
exampleSteps: Searching for the victim’s public model is reconnaissance.
Building a surrogate to craft attacks offline is preparation of an attack.
Each step maps to a technique, which gives defenders places to detect or interrupt it.
mls-u1-concept-10.takeaway: ATLAS describes how attacks unfold as a sequence of steps.

mls-u1-concept-11.title: The OWASP LLM Top 10
mls-u1-concept-11.body: The OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications lists the most important risks for applications built on language models, including prompt injection, sensitive information disclosure, improper output handling and excessive agency. It is a prioritised risk list for builders, not a complete taxonomy of attacks.
mls-u1-concept-11.example: A team building a support chatbot reviews the list before launch.
exampleSteps: Prompt injection prompts a review of what the bot reads.
Excessive agency prompts a review of what the bot is allowed to do.
mls-u1-concept-11.takeaway: Use the list to check that common application risks have an owner.

mls-u1-concept-12.title: Drawing trust boundaries
mls-u1-concept-12.body: A trust boundary is any point where data or control passes between parties that trust each other differently. In ML systems these include training data sources, third-party weights, retrieved documents, and users. Each crossing needs a named assumption and a control.
mls-u1-concept-12.example: A support assistant answers from a help centre and customer emails.
exampleSteps: Help articles are written by staff and cross a low-risk boundary.
Customer emails are written by anyone and cross a high-risk boundary.
The assistant must not treat text in those emails as instructions.
mls-u1-concept-12.takeaway: Find where untrusted data enters, then decide what it is allowed to influence.

mls-u1-concept-13.title: Attack success rate
mls-u1-concept-13.body: Attack success rate is the fraction of attempts where the attacker reaches the goal. For evasion, count only inputs the model handled correctly before the attack, otherwise inputs that were already wrong inflate the score.
mls-u1-concept-13.example: An attack runs on 400 correctly classified inputs and 300 become misclassified.
exampleSteps: Successes are \(300\) out of \(400\) attempts.
mls-u1-concept-13.takeaway: Report the denominator with every attack success rate.

mls-u1-concept-14.title: Clean and robust accuracy
mls-u1-concept-14.body: Clean accuracy is measured on unmodified data. Accuracy under a stated attack and budget is an empirical estimate of robust accuracy. True robust accuracy requires correctness for every allowed perturbation; a tested attack can miss failures, so its result can overestimate robustness. Always name the attack, budget and evaluation set.
mls-u1-concept-14.formula: \[\text{accuracy under attack} = \frac{\text{correct after attack}}{\text{total test inputs}}\]
mls-u1-concept-14.example: On 500 images, 480 are correct when clean and 150 remain correct under attack.
exampleSteps: Clean accuracy is \(480/500 = 96\%\).
Robust accuracy is \(150/500 = 30\%\).
mls-u1-concept-14.takeaway: Always quote robust accuracy together with the attack and budget used.

mls-u1-concept-15.title: Expected loss
mls-u1-concept-15.body: Risk combines how likely an event is with how much it costs. Multiplying the two gives an expected loss, which helps compare threats and decide whether a defence is worth paying for. The estimates are rough, but writing them down makes the assumptions open to challenge.
mls-u1-concept-15.example: An attack has a 5% yearly chance of causing a loss of 20,000 euros.
exampleSteps: A control costing much more than 1,000 euros a year needs a stronger justification.
mls-u1-concept-15.takeaway: Compare the cost of a control with the loss it is expected to avoid.

mls-u1-concept-16.title: Detectors and base rates
mls-u1-concept-16.body: Attacks are usually rare, so even an accurate detector can raise mostly false alarms. Precision depends on how common attacks are, and that matters for anyone who has to act on the alerts.
mls-u1-concept-16.example: Attacks make up 10% of traffic, and a detector has TPR 0.8 and FPR 0.1.
exampleSteps: True alerts per input: \(0.8 \times 0.1 = 0.08\).
False alerts per input: \(0.1 \times 0.9 = 0.09\).
Precision is \(0.08/0.17 \approx 0.47\).
mls-u1-concept-16.takeaway: Evaluate a detector at the attack rate you expect in production.

mls-u2-concept-01.title: What an adversarial example is
mls-u2-concept-01.body: In the small-perturbation image setting, an adversarial example is deliberately changed to make a model give a wrong output while preserving the image’s true label. The change is limited by a budget \(\epsilon\) under a chosen norm. Other threat models allow visible patches or other changes; a small norm alone does not guarantee perceptual similarity.
mls-u2-concept-01.example: An image of a panda is classified correctly.
exampleSteps: A tiny, structured pattern \(\delta\) is added to every pixel.
People still see a panda, while the model reports a different animal with high confidence.
mls-u2-concept-01.takeaway: The perturbation is optimised against the model. It is not random noise.

mls-u2-concept-02.title: Measuring perturbations
mls-u2-concept-02.body: Norms define what small means. The \(L_\infty\) norm is the largest change to any feature, \(L_2\) is the Euclidean length, and \(L_0\) counts how many features changed. The choice describes the attacker: many tiny changes, or a few large ones.
exampleSteps: \(\|\delta\|_\infty = 0.08\), the largest absolute entry.
\(\|\delta\|_0 = 2\), since two entries are nonzero.
mls-u2-concept-02.takeaway: A robustness claim is only meaningful for the norm and budget it names.

mls-u2-concept-03.title: Why linear models are enough
mls-u2-concept-03.body: High dimensionality makes tiny changes add up. For a linear score \(w^\top x\), moving each feature by \(\epsilon\) in the direction of \(\text{sign}(w_i)\) raises the score by \(\epsilon\|w\|_1\). Many small coordinated moves produce a large change even though each one is invisible.
exampleSteps: The score can change by \(0.5 \times 3 = 1.5\).
mls-u2-concept-03.takeaway: Adversarial vulnerability does not require a complicated model.

mls-u2-concept-04.title: Attacks as optimisation
mls-u2-concept-04.body: Training adjusts the weights to reduce loss. An evasion attack holds the weights fixed and adjusts the input to increase loss, staying inside the budget. Backpropagation gives the gradient with respect to the input just as easily as with respect to the weights.
mls-u2-concept-04.example: The same loss is used in two opposite ways.
exampleSteps: Training: fix \(x\), update \(\theta\) downhill.
Attacking: fix \(\theta\), update \(x\) uphill.
mls-u2-concept-04.takeaway: An evasion attack is training turned around to act on the input.

mls-u2-concept-05.title: The fast gradient sign method
mls-u2-concept-05.body: FGSM takes one step of size \(\epsilon\) in the sign of the input gradient. It is cheap, and it is a useful first test. It is also a weak attack, so surviving it proves very little.
exampleSteps: The signs are \((+1,-1)\).
mls-u2-concept-05.takeaway: FGSM ignores the size of the gradient and uses only its sign.

mls-u2-concept-06.title: Targeted gradient attacks
mls-u2-concept-06.body: To force a chosen class \(t\), the attacker lowers the loss computed against \(t\), so the step goes against the gradient. The sign flips compared with the untargeted case, where the attacker raises the loss for the true label.
mls-u2-concept-06.example: An attacker wants a cat image labelled as a dog.
exampleSteps: Compute the loss as if dog were the correct label.
Step in the direction that makes the model more confident in dog.
mls-u2-concept-06.takeaway: Untargeted attacks climb the true label’s loss. Targeted attacks descend the target’s loss.

mls-u2-concept-07.title: Projected gradient descent
mls-u2-concept-07.body: PGD repeats small gradient steps and, after each one, projects the result back into the allowed region around the original input. For an \(L_\infty\) budget, projection simply clips each feature to \([x_i-\epsilon, x_i+\epsilon]\). It is a standard strong first-order attack.
mls-u2-concept-07.example: The original feature is \(0.40\), \(\epsilon=0.05\), and a step reaches \(0.47\).
exampleSteps: The allowed range is \([0.35, 0.45]\).
\(0.47\) is projected to \(0.45\).
mls-u2-concept-07.takeaway: PGD explores within the budget and never leaves it.

mls-u2-concept-08.title: Constraints in the real world
mls-u2-concept-08.body: Real attackers cannot change arbitrary features. Pixels must stay in a valid range, malware must still run, and a printed sticker must survive changes of angle and light. Physical attacks optimise over many transformations so that the result works on average.
mls-u2-concept-08.example: An attacker adds a patch to a road sign.
exampleSteps: The optimisation samples many viewing angles and lighting conditions.
A patch that succeeds only from one angle is discarded by this process.
mls-u2-concept-08.takeaway: Realistic evaluations use the constraints a real attacker faces.

mls-u2-concept-09.title: Transferability
mls-u2-concept-09.body: Adversarial examples crafted on one model often fool a different model trained for the same task. An attacker can train a surrogate, attack it with full gradient access, then send the results to the real target. This makes hidden weights a weaker protection than they appear.
mls-u2-concept-09.example: A company hides its classifier behind an API.
exampleSteps: An attacker labels public images by querying the API.
They train a surrogate on those labels and attack the surrogate locally.
Many of the resulting images also fool the original.
mls-u2-concept-09.takeaway: A private model can still be attacked using a public one.

mls-u2-concept-10.title: Estimating gradients with scores
mls-u2-concept-10.body: If an API returns confidence scores, the attacker can estimate the gradient with finite differences. Nudging one feature up and down and comparing the two scores approximates the partial derivative for that feature.
exampleSteps: The difference is \(0.02\) and \(2h=0.02\).
The estimated partial derivative is \(1\).
mls-u2-concept-10.takeaway: Detailed confidence scores leak gradient information.

mls-u2-concept-11.title: The query budget
mls-u2-concept-11.body: Finite differences cost two queries per feature per gradient estimate, so naive attacks are expensive for high-dimensional inputs. Practical attacks use random directions to estimate a gradient with far fewer queries, but counting queries still shows why rate limits raise the attacker’s cost.
mls-u2-concept-11.example: An input has 100 features and the attack runs 10 steps.
exampleSteps: \(2 \times 100 \times 10 = 2000\) queries.
mls-u2-concept-11.takeaway: Query count is a useful measure of black-box attack cost.

mls-u2-concept-12.title: Label-only attacks
mls-u2-concept-12.body: Hiding confidence scores does not stop attacks. Decision-based attacks begin from an input that is already misclassified and walk along the decision boundary, moving closer to the original while staying misclassified. They use only the final label, at the cost of many queries.
mls-u2-concept-12.example: An API returns only the words approve or decline.
exampleSteps: Start from an application that already receives the outcome the attacker wants.
Move it step by step towards the real application, keeping only the moves that retain that outcome.
mls-u2-concept-12.takeaway: Returning only labels raises the cost but does not close the attack.

mls-u2-concept-13.title: Adversarial training
mls-u2-concept-13.body: Adversarial training generates attacks during training and fits the model to them, which turns learning into a min-max problem. It is one of the most reliable empirical defences, but it raises training cost, often lowers clean accuracy, and covers mainly the threat model it was trained on.
mls-u2-concept-13.example: A team hardens an image model.
exampleSteps: At each batch, PGD finds strong perturbations for the current weights.
The weights are updated on those perturbed inputs.
mls-u2-concept-13.takeaway: Adversarial training buys robustness with compute and some clean accuracy.

mls-u2-concept-14.title: Gradient masking
mls-u2-concept-14.body: Some defences only make gradients unhelpful, for example through shattered, randomised or vanishing gradients. Gradient attacks then fail although adversarial examples still exist. A warning sign is that black-box or transfer attacks work better than white-box ones, which should not happen in a sound evaluation.
mls-u2-concept-14.example: A new defence reports 95% robust accuracy under PGD.
exampleSteps: Testers try a transfer attack from an undefended surrogate.
Robust accuracy falls to 10%, so the first result reflected a failing attack.
mls-u2-concept-14.takeaway: If a weaker attacker does better, the evaluation is broken.

mls-u2-concept-15.title: Adaptive evaluation
mls-u2-concept-15.body: A defence should be tested with attacks designed specifically to defeat it, assuming the attacker knows how it works. Many published detectors and defences have fallen to such adaptive attacks after appearing strong against generic ones.
mls-u2-concept-15.example: A defence adds a detector that flags odd inputs.
exampleSteps: A generic attack ignores the detector and gets flagged.
An adaptive attack optimises to fool the classifier and the detector together.
mls-u2-concept-15.takeaway: An evaluation is only as strong as the attacker it imagines.

mls-u2-concept-16.title: Certified robustness
mls-u2-concept-16.body: Gaussian randomised smoothing defines a smoothed classifier as the most probable class of a base classifier under isotropic noise \(\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma^2 I)\), with \(\sigma>0\). Let \(\underline p_A>1/2\) be a valid lower bound on that class probability. Using \(1-\underline p_A\) as a conservative bound for every rival gives the radius below; \(\Phi\) is the standard normal CDF. A Monte Carlo certificate needs a statistically valid lower confidence bound, not the observed vote fraction: its confidence is \(1-\alpha\). If the bound is at most \(1/2\), this procedure abstains. The guarantee fixes the smoothed prediction for all \(\|\delta\|_2<R\); it does not certify the base classifier, correctness of the label, or safety outside this threat model.
mls-u2-concept-16.example: Using isotropic Gaussian noise with \(\sigma=0.5\), suppose a valid lower confidence bound satisfies \(\Phi^{-1}(\underline p_A)=1\).
exampleSteps: At the confidence level of the bound, every perturbation with \(L_2\) norm strictly below \(0.5\) leaves the smoothed classifier’s prediction unchanged. This does not prove that prediction is correct.
mls-u2-concept-16.takeaway: A certificate needs a stated classifier, noise distribution, probability bound and perturbation set.

mls-u3-concept-01.title: Kinds of poisoning
mls-u3-concept-01.body: Poisoning alters training so the finished model misbehaves. Availability poisoning degrades the model in general. Targeted poisoning changes the result for chosen inputs. Backdoor poisoning plants a trigger that activates bad behaviour on demand. The last two can leave normal accuracy almost unchanged.
exampleSteps: One injects junk until overall accuracy collapses: availability.
One makes a single rival’s product get misclassified: targeted.
One makes any input with a certain pattern get approved: backdoor.
mls-u3-concept-01.takeaway: Poisoned models that behave normally on tests are the dangerous ones.

mls-u3-concept-02.title: Clean-label poisoning
mls-u3-concept-02.body: In clean-label poisoning, every poisoned record has a correct label and looks legitimate to a reviewer. Small feature changes place it close to a chosen target in the model’s internal representation, so the decision boundary shifts around that target.
mls-u3-concept-02.example: An attacker wants one specific image misclassified.
exampleSteps: They craft images of the desired class that look normal and carry the correct label.
In feature space, those images sit next to the target.
After training, the target falls on the wrong side of the boundary.
mls-u3-concept-02.takeaway: Reviewing labels does not detect every poisoning attack.

mls-u3-concept-03.title: Poisoning at web scale
mls-u3-concept-03.body: Large datasets are often distributed as lists of URLs. If a domain expires, anyone can buy it and serve different content to later downloaders. Periodic snapshots of editable sites can similarly be timed so that malicious edits are captured. Researchers showed that both are cheap in practice.
mls-u3-concept-03.example: A dataset index points to an image on an expired domain.
exampleSteps: The attacker registers the domain for a small fee.
Later users download the attacker’s image, unaware that it differs from what was indexed.
mls-u3-concept-03.takeaway: A list of URLs is not a fixed dataset unless the content is verified.

mls-u3-concept-04.title: How little data is needed
mls-u3-concept-04.body: The share of a dataset an attacker must control can be surprisingly small, and it need not scale up with the dataset. A 2025 study found that a near-constant number of documents, around 250, was enough to install a simple backdoor across language models of several sizes. Small absolute access can matter.
mls-u3-concept-04.example: An attacker adds 100 records to a set of 200,000.
exampleSteps: The poison rate is \(100/200000 = 0.05\%\).
A tiny percentage is not proof of safety, because the absolute count may be what matters.
mls-u3-concept-04.takeaway: Do not dismiss poisoning because the percentage looks small.

mls-u3-concept-05.title: How backdoors work
mls-u3-concept-05.body: A backdoored model learns two behaviours: the normal task, and a rule that maps a hidden trigger to the attacker’s chosen output. Because the trigger is absent from ordinary test data, standard evaluation shows a healthy model.
mls-u3-concept-05.example: A vision model is poisoned with a small yellow square.
exampleSteps: Images without the square are classified normally.
Any image with the square is reported as the attacker’s chosen class.
mls-u3-concept-05.takeaway: A clean test set cannot reveal a trigger it does not contain.

mls-u3-concept-06.title: Measuring a backdoor
mls-u3-concept-06.body: A backdoor has two figures: clean accuracy on normal inputs, and attack success rate on inputs that carry the trigger. A strong backdoor has high values for both. When testing a suspected trigger, exclude inputs that already belong to the target class.
mls-u3-concept-06.formula: \[\text{ASR}_{\text{trigger}} = \frac{\#\{\text{triggered inputs classified as target}\}}{\#\{\text{triggered non-target inputs}\}}\]
mls-u3-concept-06.example: A trigger is applied to 1,000 non-target images.
exampleSteps: 950 are classified as the attacker’s class.
mls-u3-concept-06.takeaway: Report trigger success together with clean accuracy.

mls-u3-concept-07.title: Outsourced training
mls-u3-concept-07.body: Whoever trains or supplies the weights holds full control over the model. Outsourced training and pre-trained models therefore form a trust relationship. Fine-tuning on clean data reduces some backdoors, but it does not reliably remove them.
mls-u3-concept-07.example: A startup downloads a pretrained encoder and fine-tunes the last layer.
exampleSteps: The hidden layers are unchanged and may still respond to a trigger.
The startup’s clean validation data shows no sign of it.
mls-u3-concept-07.takeaway: Treat pretrained weights as code from their author.

mls-u3-concept-08.title: Backdoors in language models
mls-u3-concept-08.body: Language models can be trained to behave normally until a trigger appears, such as a certain phrase or a stated date. Research on sleeper agents showed that such behaviour can persist through standard safety training, which may produce a model that only looks clean.
mls-u3-concept-08.example: A research model writes safe code when the prompt states one year.
exampleSteps: When the prompt states a different year, it inserts vulnerabilities.
Safety training on prompts without the trigger leaves this behaviour in place.
mls-u3-concept-08.takeaway: Passing behavioural safety tests does not rule out a hidden trigger.

mls-u3-concept-09.title: Provenance and lineage
mls-u3-concept-09.body: Provenance records where data came from, who changed it, and which training run used it. Hashes and versioned manifests show that a dataset has not changed since it was recorded. That does not make the data trustworthy, but it allows audits, and it tells you what to retrain after a compromise.
mls-u3-concept-09.example: An incident reveals that one data vendor was compromised in March.
exampleSteps: With lineage, the team can list exactly which models consumed that vendor’s data.
Without it, every model has to be treated as suspect.
mls-u3-concept-09.takeaway: You cannot clean up what you cannot trace.

mls-u3-concept-10.title: Robust statistics
mls-u3-concept-10.body: An average can be dragged arbitrarily far by one outlier. Robust statistics such as the median or a trimmed mean limit how much a small fraction of bad data can move the result. Many data sanitisation and aggregation defences build on this idea.
mls-u3-concept-10.example: Nine sensors read 10 and one compromised sensor reads 110.
exampleSteps: The median is \(10\), unaffected by the outlier.
mls-u3-concept-10.takeaway: Choose estimators that a small minority cannot control.

mls-u3-concept-11.title: Detecting poisoned data
mls-u3-concept-11.body: Poisoned examples can leave statistical traces in a model’s internal representations. Spectral methods look for an unusual direction in the features of a class and remove the examples that align with it. These methods help, but attackers can adapt, and clean-looking results are not a guarantee.
mls-u3-concept-11.example: Feature vectors for one class are collected after training.
exampleSteps: The top singular direction is computed.
Examples with outlying projections are removed and the model is retrained.
mls-u3-concept-11.takeaway: Detection reduces risk. It does not certify a clean model.

mls-u3-concept-12.title: Limiting the feedback loop
mls-u3-concept-12.body: Systems that learn continuously from users give attackers an ongoing channel into training. Useful controls include holding data before use, limiting each account’s influence, requiring review for high-impact samples, and comparing new models with the current one before promotion.
mls-u3-concept-12.example: A review site’s ranking model retrains daily on new ratings.
exampleSteps: Each account’s contribution is capped.
New models run alongside the current one, and large shifts for a single product block promotion.
mls-u3-concept-12.takeaway: Limit how fast and how much any one source can change the model.

mls-u4-concept-01.title: Membership inference
mls-u4-concept-01.body: A membership inference attack decides whether a specific record was in the training set. Being in a dataset can itself be sensitive, as with a clinical trial. Models often behave differently on records they were trained on, and that difference is the signal.
mls-u4-concept-01.example: A model is trained on patients with a given diagnosis.
exampleSteps: An attacker holding someone’s record queries the model.
If the record looks like a training member, the attacker learns the person probably has that diagnosis.
mls-u4-concept-01.takeaway: Membership alone can be private information.

mls-u4-concept-02.title: Overfitting as a signal
mls-u4-concept-02.body: Overfit models tend to be more confident and have lower loss on training data than on new data. A simple attack compares the loss on a target record with a threshold. Shadow models trained on similar data help an attacker choose that threshold or calibrate per-record behaviour.
mls-u4-concept-02.example: A record has loss \(0.02\), and the threshold is \(\tau=0.1\).
exampleSteps: The attack predicts that the record was in the training set.
mls-u4-concept-02.takeaway: The train-test gap is a privacy leak as well as a quality problem.

mls-u4-concept-03.title: Measuring membership risk
mls-u4-concept-03.body: Membership advantage is the true positive rate minus the false positive rate. Average figures can hide the real risk, so strong evaluations report the true positive rate at a very low false positive rate, which asks whether the attack can confidently identify at least some individuals.
mls-u4-concept-03.example: An attack has TPR 0.5 and FPR 0.3.
exampleSteps: The advantage is \(0.5 - 0.3 = 0.2\).
Random guessing has TPR equal to FPR, which gives an advantage of \(0\).
mls-u4-concept-03.takeaway: Check low-FPR performance, because that is where confident leaks show up.

mls-u4-concept-04.title: Inversion and attribute inference
mls-u4-concept-04.body: Model inversion uses outputs to reconstruct representative features of a class or of training data. Attribute inference uses partial knowledge of a person plus model outputs to infer a hidden attribute. Both turn a model into a source of information that was never meant to be released.
mls-u4-concept-04.example: An attacker knows a patient’s demographics and a model’s dosage recommendation.
exampleSteps: They test which hidden genetic marker values best explain that recommendation.
The output has leaked an attribute that was never entered by the attacker.
mls-u4-concept-04.takeaway: Outputs correlated with sensitive attributes can reveal those attributes.

mls-u4-concept-05.title: Memorisation in language models
mls-u4-concept-05.body: Language models can reproduce training text verbatim, including personal data or secrets. Researchers extracted such sequences through queries to deployed and open models. Rare or repeated strings are memorised more easily, and output filters may not catch all of them.
mls-u4-concept-05.example: A training corpus contains a contact block that is repeated in many documents.
exampleSteps: The model is prompted with the first part of that block.
It completes the block with the remaining personal details.
mls-u4-concept-05.takeaway: Data given to a model during training may come back out.

mls-u4-concept-06.title: Canaries
mls-u4-concept-06.body: A canary is a unique fake secret deliberately planted in training data. After training, the team checks whether the model can reproduce it. Canaries give a concrete, measurable test of memorisation, and they can be checked again after each pipeline change.
mls-u4-concept-06.example: A team inserts 20 fake account numbers before training.
exampleSteps: After training, each is prompted with its prefix.
3 are completed correctly, so the pipeline demonstrably memorises rare strings.
mls-u4-concept-06.takeaway: Measure memorisation directly, using secrets you can safely plant.

mls-u4-concept-07.title: Embeddings are personal data too
mls-u4-concept-07.body: An embedding is a numeric summary of text or images, not an anonymised form of it. Research has shown that text can be reconstructed from embeddings with considerable accuracy. A vector database holding embeddings of private documents needs the same protection as those documents.
mls-u4-concept-07.example: A team stores embeddings of support tickets and treats them as safe to share.
exampleSteps: An attacker with access to the vectors trains a decoder.
The decoder recovers names and details from the tickets.
mls-u4-concept-07.takeaway: Protect embeddings at the level of the data they came from.

mls-u4-concept-08.title: Leakage from shared gradients
mls-u4-concept-08.body: Federated learning shares gradients instead of raw data, but gradients depend on that data. For one example in a scalar-output linear model with a bias and a nonzero bias gradient, the input can be recovered exactly: dividing the weight gradient by the bias gradient gives the input.
mls-u4-concept-08.example: The weight gradient is \((4, 2)\) and \(\partial\ell/\partial b = 2\).
exampleSteps: Dividing each component by \(2\) gives \(x = (2, 1)\).
mls-u4-concept-08.takeaway: Sharing gradients is not the same as keeping data private.

mls-u4-concept-09.title: Definition of differential privacy
mls-u4-concept-09.body: A randomised algorithm is differentially private if adding or removing one person’s record barely changes the distribution of its output. The parameter \(\epsilon\) limits that change, and \(\delta\) is a small additive slack in the probability inequality, not a per-record probability of a privacy breach. The inequality must hold for every pair of neighbouring datasets and every output event. Smaller \(\epsilon\) means stronger privacy.
exampleSteps: No output can be more than twice as likely with a record as without it.
mls-u4-concept-09.takeaway: Differential privacy bounds what any one record can change.

mls-u4-concept-10.title: The Laplace mechanism
mls-u4-concept-10.body: To release a numeric result privately, add Laplace noise with scale set by the query’s sensitivity \(\Delta\), which is the most one record can change the result, divided by \(\epsilon\). Stronger privacy or higher sensitivity both mean more noise.
exampleSteps: Noise drawn from a Laplace distribution with scale \(10\) is added to the count.
mls-u4-concept-10.takeaway: Noise is calibrated to how much one record can matter.

mls-u4-concept-11.title: DP-SGD
mls-u4-concept-11.body: DP-SGD bounds the influence of each example, then hides what remains. Each per-example gradient is clipped to norm at most \(C\), the clipped gradients are summed, and Gaussian noise is added. Clipping provides the sensitivity bound that the noise depends on.
exampleSteps: \(\|g\|_2 = 5\), which gives a scale factor of \(1/5\).
The clipped gradient is \((0.6, 0.8)\).
mls-u4-concept-11.takeaway: Clip each example first, then add noise.

mls-u4-concept-12.title: Privacy budgets
mls-u4-concept-12.body: Every differentially private release consumes privacy. Under basic composition, the \(\epsilon\) values of successive releases add up. Tighter accounting gives better numbers in practice, but the principle remains: repeated access has a cumulative cost, and more privacy usually means lower accuracy.
exampleSteps: By basic composition, the total is at most \(4 \times 0.5 = 2\).
mls-u4-concept-12.takeaway: Track the total privacy spent, not just the cost of each query.

mls-u4-concept-13.title: Equation-solving extraction
mls-u4-concept-13.body: Prediction APIs can reveal enough to reconstruct a model. A logistic regression has \(d+1\) parameters, and each returned confidence gives one linear equation after applying the logit. With enough independent queries, the attacker can solve for the weights exactly.
exampleSteps: Unknowns are \(3\) weights and \(1\) bias, for \(4\) in total.
Four independent queries with exact confidences determine the model.
mls-u4-concept-13.takeaway: Exact confidence scores can give away the model’s parameters.

mls-u4-concept-14.title: Surrogate models
mls-u4-concept-14.body: For complex models, attackers often do not try to recover the exact weights. They use the API’s answers as labels to train a surrogate with similar behaviour, avoiding the cost of data collection and labelling. The result can be used directly or to develop attacks offline.
mls-u4-concept-14.example: An attacker sends a large set of public images to a paid classifier.
exampleSteps: The responses become a labelled dataset.
Training on that dataset gives a local model with similar functionality.
mls-u4-concept-14.takeaway: The API’s output is a labelling service for anyone who queries it.

mls-u4-concept-15.title: Limiting extraction
mls-u4-concept-15.body: API design affects extraction cost. Rounding or removing confidence values, restricting optional outputs such as logit controls and log probabilities, and watching for systematic query patterns all raise the bar. In 2024, researchers recovered the output embedding projection layer, up to symmetries, of some production language models through such API features.
mls-u4-concept-15.example: An API offers detailed log probabilities and a per-token logit bias parameter.
exampleSteps: Together, they provided precise measurements about the last layer of the model.
The providers changed these API features after being notified.
mls-u4-concept-15.takeaway: Every extra output field gives attackers additional information.

mls-u4-concept-16.title: Watermarks and fingerprints
mls-u4-concept-16.body: Watermarks embed a verifiable signal in a model, or in its outputs, so that ownership or origin can later be argued. They support detection and legal claims after the fact. They do not prevent copying, and retraining or paraphrasing can weaken them.
mls-u4-concept-16.example: A provider watermarks the text its model generates.
exampleSteps: A detector can later test text for the statistical signal.
Heavy paraphrasing weakens the signal, so a negative result does not prove the text was human-written.
mls-u4-concept-16.takeaway: Watermarks help with attribution. They are not access control.

mls-u5-concept-01.title: Instructions and data share a channel
mls-u5-concept-01.body: A language model receives its instructions and its data as one stream of tokens, and it has no reliable way to tell them apart. Prompt injection exploits this: text that should be treated as data is treated as a command. Unlike SQL injection, there is no equivalent of a parameterised query.
mls-u5-concept-01.example: An application asks a model to translate a customer message.
exampleSteps: The message contains a sentence asking the model to do something else.
Nothing structural marks that sentence as data, so the model may follow it.
mls-u5-concept-01.takeaway: Prompt injection follows from how language models read their input.

mls-u5-concept-02.title: Direct and indirect injection
mls-u5-concept-02.body: In direct injection, the attacker types into the application themselves. In indirect injection, the instructions are hidden in content that the model later reads, such as a web page, an email or a document. Indirect injection is dangerous because the victim is a legitimate user who did nothing unusual.
mls-u5-concept-02.example: An assistant summarises a user’s inbox.
exampleSteps: A stranger sends an email containing hidden instructions.
The user asks for a summary, and the model reads the attacker’s text.
mls-u5-concept-02.takeaway: Any content a model reads can act as an attack payload.

mls-u5-concept-03.title: Injection and jailbreaks
mls-u5-concept-03.body: A jailbreak tries to get a model to break its safety training, usually producing content it would otherwise refuse. Prompt injection attacks the application built around the model, by overriding what the developer intended. They use similar techniques, but they have different victims and different fixes.
mls-u5-concept-03.example: Two incidents occur in one week.
exampleSteps: A user persuades a chatbot to write prohibited content: a jailbreak.
A web page makes an agent forward a user’s files: prompt injection.
mls-u5-concept-03.takeaway: Ask who is harmed and whose intent was overridden.

mls-u5-concept-04.title: System prompts are not secrets
mls-u5-concept-04.body: A system prompt shapes behaviour but does not enforce it, and users can often extract it. Credentials, connection strings, and authorisation rules therefore should not depend on the prompt staying secret. Permissions belong in code that the model cannot alter.
mls-u5-concept-04.example: A bot’s prompt says that only managers may see salaries, and it holds a database password.
exampleSteps: A user coaxes the model into printing the password.
The rule about managers is only a suggestion to the model.
mls-u5-concept-04.takeaway: Assume the system prompt will be read. Enforce rules outside the model.

mls-u5-concept-05.title: The lethal trifecta
mls-u5-concept-05.body: A serious data theft becomes possible when one system combines three things: access to private data, exposure to untrusted content, and a way to communicate externally. Injected instructions in the content can tell the model to read the data and send it out. Removing any one leg blocks this path.
mls-u5-concept-05.example: An assistant reads private files and browses the web.
exampleSteps: A malicious page tells it to put file contents into a URL.
The browsing tool requests that URL, and the data reaches the attacker’s server.
mls-u5-concept-05.takeaway: Check every agent for all three legs at once.

mls-u5-concept-06.title: Exfiltration through rendering
mls-u5-concept-06.body: Data can leave without any explicit tool. If a chat interface automatically loads images from model-generated Markdown, the model can place secrets in an image URL, and the browser sends them when it fetches the image. Restricting which domains can be loaded closes this common path.
mls-u5-concept-06.example: The model outputs an image link to an attacker’s domain, with a secret in the query string.
exampleSteps: The user’s browser loads the image with no click.
The attacker’s server logs the request, including the secret.
mls-u5-concept-06.takeaway: Treat auto-loaded links in model output as an outbound channel.

mls-u5-concept-07.title: Improper output handling
mls-u5-concept-07.body: Model output is untrusted input to whatever consumes it. If it reaches a browser, a shell or a database without the normal protections, classic vulnerabilities such as XSS, command injection and SQL injection return, now reachable through a prompt.
mls-u5-concept-07.example: An app inserts model output into a page as raw HTML.
exampleSteps: An attacker injects instructions so that the model emits a script tag.
The script runs in the victim’s session, which is cross-site scripting.
mls-u5-concept-07.takeaway: Validate and encode model output exactly as you would user input.

mls-u5-concept-08.title: Unbounded consumption
mls-u5-concept-08.body: Language model requests are expensive, and their cost depends on input and output length. Without limits, an attacker can exhaust capacity or run up large bills. Controls include per-user quotas, maximum token limits, timeouts and spending alerts.
mls-u5-concept-08.example: 100 requests use 10,000 output tokens each, at $10 per million tokens.
exampleSteps: Total tokens: \(100 \times 10000 = 1000000\).
Cost: \(1 \times 10 = 10\) dollars.
mls-u5-concept-08.takeaway: Put limits on tokens and spend, not only on the request count.

mls-u5-concept-09.title: Retrieved text is untrusted
mls-u5-concept-09.body: Retrieval-augmented generation pulls documents into the prompt to answer a question. Each retrieved passage becomes model input, so anyone able to write to the knowledge base can influence the answer or inject instructions. Internal does not mean trusted when many people can edit a page.
mls-u5-concept-09.example: A company wiki can be edited by every employee and all contractors.
exampleSteps: A contractor’s account is compromised and a page is altered.
Everyone whose questions retrieve that page receives the attacker’s content.
mls-u5-concept-09.takeaway: Know who can write to everything your model can retrieve.

mls-u5-concept-10.title: Knowledge poisoning
mls-u5-concept-10.body: An attacker can plant passages crafted to be retrieved for a chosen question and to produce a chosen answer. An attack has two conditions: the text must rank highly for the question, and it must then steer the model. A small number of passages can be enough.
mls-u5-concept-10.example: An attacker targets the question of who should be paid for an invoice.
exampleSteps: They add a document that closely matches the wording of that question.
The document states a fraudulent bank account as the right answer.
mls-u5-concept-10.takeaway: Attackers optimise for the retriever as well as for the model.

mls-u5-concept-11.title: Permissions in retrieval
mls-u5-concept-11.body: The model cannot be relied on to hide what it has already been shown. Access control must apply before retrieved content reaches the prompt, using the requesting user’s permissions. Filtering the answer afterwards is too late.
mls-u5-concept-11.example: A shared index holds documents from both HR and engineering.
exampleSteps: An engineer asks about salary bands.
The query is filtered to documents the engineer can access, so HR files are never retrieved.
mls-u5-concept-11.takeaway: Filter by the user’s permissions before text reaches the model.

mls-u5-concept-12.title: Similarity can be gamed
mls-u5-concept-12.body: Retrievers typically rank passages by cosine similarity between embedding vectors. It is a measure of direction, chosen for relevance and not for safety, and an attacker who can craft text can try to maximise it for chosen queries.
exampleSteps: \(u^\top v = 0.8\) and both vectors have length \(1\).
The similarity is \(0.8\).
mls-u5-concept-12.takeaway: A high retrieval score means similar, and says nothing about trustworthy.

mls-u5-concept-13.title: Filters are probabilistic
mls-u5-concept-13.body: Input and output classifiers catch many attacks, but they are statistical, and an attacker can retry. If each attempt independently evades detection with probability \(q\), the chance of at least one success in \(k\) attempts grows quickly. Rate limits and account action reduce \(k\).
exampleSteps: The probability of at least one success is \(0.19\).
mls-u5-concept-13.takeaway: A filter that stops most attempts can still lose to a persistent attacker.

mls-u5-concept-14.title: Marking untrusted content
mls-u5-concept-14.body: Delimiters, tags, and techniques such as spotlighting help a model recognise which text came from outside. These measurably reduce the success of injection, and they are cheap. They are still only a signal to the model, so they should not be the only defence for risky actions.
mls-u5-concept-14.example: Retrieved text is wrapped and transformed so that the model can recognise it.
exampleSteps: The system prompt says that marked text is data and never instructions.
Attack success falls in tests, but it does not reach zero.
mls-u5-concept-14.takeaway: Marking helps the model, but it does not create a boundary.

mls-u5-concept-15.title: Constraining output
mls-u5-concept-15.body: When an application needs a specific kind of result, it can require a strict schema and validate it in code: fixed fields, allowed values, and ranges. An injected model then has far less room to cause harm, because anything outside the schema is rejected.
mls-u5-concept-15.example: A triage model must return a category and a priority.
exampleSteps: The category must be one of five values, and the priority must be a number from 1 to 3.
Free text aimed at a downstream system is rejected at validation.
mls-u5-concept-15.takeaway: Narrow outputs mean narrow attack paths.

mls-u5-concept-16.title: Testing like an attacker
mls-u5-concept-16.body: Security testing for LLM applications means adversarial test suites run repeatedly, not a one-time check. Because outputs vary, each case should be run many times. Track attack success and ordinary task success together, so that a defence is not simply breaking the product.
mls-u5-concept-16.example: A team changes its system prompt.
exampleSteps: An automated suite replays hundreds of known injection patterns several times each.
Attack success falls from 12% to 4%, while normal task completion stays at 97%.
mls-u5-concept-16.takeaway: Measure both security and usefulness, on every change.

mls-u6-concept-01.title: Excessive agency
mls-u6-concept-01.body: An agent runs a language model in a loop with tools, so a wrong output becomes a real action. Excessive agency has three common sources: too much functionality, too many permissions, and too much autonomy. Each one should be reduced to what the task needs.
mls-u6-concept-01.example: An agent only needs to read tickets, but it uses a general admin connector.
exampleSteps: Functionality: the connector can also delete tickets.
Permissions: it runs with an administrator token.
Autonomy: nobody reviews what it does.
mls-u6-concept-01.takeaway: Give agents the fewest tools, the narrowest scopes and the least autonomy that will do.

mls-u6-concept-02.title: The confused deputy
mls-u6-concept-02.body: A confused deputy is a privileged program tricked into misusing its authority on someone else’s behalf. An agent holding a broad service account is a natural example: a low-privilege user or a malicious document can steer it into doing what they could not do themselves.
mls-u6-concept-02.example: A support agent runs with a service account that can read all customer records.
exampleSteps: A customer asks about another customer’s account.
The agent complies, because the request passes under its own broad authority.
mls-u6-concept-02.takeaway: Act with the end user’s permissions, not with the agent’s.

mls-u6-concept-03.title: Tools as an attack surface
mls-u6-concept-03.body: Agents read tool names and descriptions as text, so a malicious tool or server can hide instructions in its metadata. A tool definition can also change after it was approved. Connecting a third-party tool is therefore a supply-chain decision that also affects the prompt.
mls-u6-concept-03.example: A user installs a third-party calculator server for an agent.
exampleSteps: Its description quietly tells the model to read a local file first.
The model obeys it, although the user sees only a calculator being used.
mls-u6-concept-03.takeaway: Review and pin tools, because their descriptions are also prompts.

mls-u6-concept-04.title: Memory as persistence
mls-u6-concept-04.body: Agents with long-term memory can store content that influences future sessions. An injection that writes to memory turns a single event into a lasting compromise. Memory writes should be limited, visible to the user, and easy to inspect and delete.
mls-u6-concept-04.example: A malicious page tells an assistant to remember a false preference.
exampleSteps: The instruction is saved to the assistant’s memory.
In later conversations, without the page, the assistant still follows it.
mls-u6-concept-04.takeaway: Treat memory written from untrusted content as untrusted.

mls-u6-concept-05.title: Breaking the trifecta by design
mls-u6-concept-05.body: Because injection cannot be reliably prevented in the model, designers can make it harmless. If an agent has read untrusted content, restrict what it can do next. For example, a session that has fetched external content can lose its ability to send data outward.
mls-u6-concept-05.example: A coding agent opens an issue written by a stranger.
exampleSteps: From that point, the session cannot reach external network addresses.
Even if it is successfully injected, there is no channel for exfiltration.
mls-u6-concept-05.takeaway: Assume that the injection works, and then limit what it can reach.

mls-u6-concept-06.title: Isolating untrusted content
mls-u6-concept-06.body: In the dual LLM pattern, a privileged model plans and uses tools but never reads untrusted text, while a quarantined model reads that text but has no tools. Systems such as CaMeL go further: control flow is derived from the trusted request, and data carries capabilities that are checked by code.
mls-u6-concept-06.example: A user asks an assistant to act on an email’s contents.
exampleSteps: The planner works only from the user’s request and refers to the email through a variable.
The quarantined model extracts fields, and these cannot change the plan.
mls-u6-concept-06.takeaway: Stop untrusted data from deciding what happens next.

mls-u6-concept-07.title: Meaningful human approval
mls-u6-concept-07.body: Human approval works only if the person understands exactly what is about to happen and sees few enough requests to pay attention. Asking for approval on every step trains people to click yes. Approval should show the real action and its arguments, and it should be reserved for high-impact steps.
mls-u6-concept-07.example: An agent wants to send a payment.
exampleSteps: A poor prompt says only: Allow the agent to continue?
A good prompt shows the amount, recipient and account, drawn from the actual tool call.
mls-u6-concept-07.takeaway: Show the real parameters, and ask only when it matters.

mls-u6-concept-08.title: Sandboxing and egress control
mls-u6-concept-08.body: An agent that runs code should do so in an isolated environment with limited filesystem access and no secrets by default. Network egress should be blocked or restricted to an allow-list. These controls work at the operating-system level, so an injected model cannot talk its way out of them.
mls-u6-concept-08.example: An agent runs tests on untrusted code in a container.
exampleSteps: Only the project directory is mounted, and no cloud credentials are present.
Outbound traffic is limited to a package mirror.
mls-u6-concept-08.takeaway: Enforce limits below the model, where text cannot change them.

mls-u7-concept-01.title: Model files can run code
mls-u7-concept-01.body: Python’s pickle format can execute arbitrary code when loaded, and many older model checkpoints use it. Loading an untrusted file can therefore compromise the machine before any inference happens. Formats such as safetensors store only tensors and do not execute code on load.
mls-u7-concept-01.example: A team downloads a checkpoint file from an unknown account.
exampleSteps: A crafted pickle runs a command during loading.
Loading in restricted mode, or using safetensors, avoids that path.
mls-u7-concept-01.takeaway: Loading a model file can be equivalent to running a program.

mls-u7-concept-02.title: Trusting model hubs
mls-u7-concept-02.body: A model hub is a distribution channel, not a guarantee of safety. Risks include look-alike names, re-registered namespaces, and repository updates after you reviewed them. Enabling remote code in a loader executes Python from the repository. Pinning a specific commit keeps you on what you reviewed.
mls-u7-concept-02.example: A project loads a model by its name, and tracks the latest version.
exampleSteps: The repository owner pushes a change.
The next deployment silently receives the new files.
mls-u7-concept-02.takeaway: Pin exact revisions, and allow remote code only after reviewing it.

mls-u7-concept-03.title: Integrity and provenance
mls-u7-concept-03.body: A matching hash shows that you have the same bytes as the source. It says nothing about whether the source was honest. Signatures and provenance records add who built the artifact and how, and these can be checked by policy. Frameworks such as SLSA and model signing tools apply this to ML.
mls-u7-concept-03.example: A model file’s hash matches the value on the publisher’s page.
exampleSteps: That proves it has not changed since that hash was published.
It does not show that the publisher’s training process was sound.
mls-u7-concept-03.takeaway: Hashes prove sameness. Provenance helps to establish origin.

mls-u7-concept-04.title: Knowing what you run
mls-u7-concept-04.body: An ML bill of materials lists models, datasets, versions and dependencies. Model cards describe intended use, limits and evaluation. When a vulnerability is disclosed, or a dataset is found to be tainted, an inventory answers the first question: are we affected?
mls-u7-concept-04.example: A library used for loading models receives a critical advisory.
exampleSteps: The team searches its bill of materials for the affected version.
Within minutes, it knows which three services need an update.
mls-u7-concept-04.takeaway: Keep an inventory before you need one.

mls-u7-concept-05.title: Traditional security still applies
mls-u7-concept-05.body: ML platforms are software with the usual weaknesses: exposed dashboards, missing authentication, and vulnerable dependencies. The 2024 ShadowRay campaign involved attackers abusing Ray clusters whose job API was reachable without authentication. Often the cheapest route to a model is the server it runs on.
mls-u7-concept-05.example: An inference cluster’s management dashboard is exposed to the internet.
exampleSteps: An attacker submits a job through it.
They gain code execution and access to model weights and API keys.
mls-u7-concept-05.takeaway: Authenticate and isolate ML infrastructure like any other production system.

mls-u7-concept-06.title: Shared hardware
mls-u7-concept-06.body: Accelerators are often shared among tenants, and memory may not be cleared between workloads. The 2024 LeftoverLocals vulnerability let a process on affected GPUs read local memory left behind by another process, which was enough to reconstruct language model responses. Isolation requires attention below the application.
mls-u7-concept-06.example: Two tenants share a GPU server.
exampleSteps: One tenant’s process reads memory that the other’s job left behind.
The application’s own permissions were never involved.
mls-u7-concept-06.takeaway: Application-level access control cannot fix hardware-level leakage.

mls-u7-concept-07.title: Prompts and logs are sensitive
mls-u7-concept-07.body: Prompts and outputs often contain personal data, code and secrets, so logs become an attractive target. Decide what to log, restrict who can read it, set retention limits, and redact where possible. A prompt debugging tool can quietly become the most sensitive database in the company.
mls-u7-concept-07.example: Engineers enable full prompt logging to debug a chatbot.
exampleSteps: Users paste contracts and customer data into the bot.
The logging system was given broad read access, intended for ordinary metrics.
mls-u7-concept-07.takeaway: Protect prompt logs at the level of the data they contain.

mls-u7-concept-08.title: Monitoring for abuse
mls-u7-concept-08.body: Useful signals include unusual query volume, systematic sweeps of inputs, repeated blocked prompts, sudden changes in the distribution of outputs, and unexpected tool calls. A drift alert does not by itself mean an attack, so alerts need follow-up that separates a changed world from a hostile user.
mls-u7-concept-08.example: One API key sends many near-identical inputs, each with tiny variations.
exampleSteps: That pattern suggests a black-box evasion or extraction attempt.
The team reviews the account and slows it down while investigating.
mls-u7-concept-08.takeaway: Monitor behaviour across a sequence of requests, not only one at a time.

mls-u7-concept-09.title: Release gates
mls-u7-concept-09.body: Models and prompts should move to production through defined checks, as code does. A release gate can require the signed artifact, an evaluation for robustness and privacy, an adversarial regression suite, and comparison with the current version. Failed checks block promotion automatically.
mls-u7-concept-09.example: A new prompt version is proposed.
exampleSteps: Automated tests replay known injections and normal tasks.
A rise in attack success blocks the release even though the demo looked good.
mls-u7-concept-09.takeaway: A change to a prompt is a production change.

mls-u7-concept-10.title: Responding to incidents
mls-u7-concept-10.body: An ML incident plan adds steps to usual incident response: roll back to a known good model, identify which data and models are affected using lineage, rotate any exposed credentials, and decide whether to retrain. Keeping previous versions makes rollback possible.
mls-u7-concept-10.example: A backdoor is found in the current production model.
exampleSteps: Serve the last verified version at once.
Use lineage to find every other model trained on the same data.
Retrain from cleaned data and add a test for the discovered trigger.
mls-u7-concept-10.takeaway: Prepare rollback and retraining paths before they are needed.

mls-u7-concept-11.title: Defence in depth
mls-u7-concept-11.body: No single control stops every attack in this course. A sound design combines limits on data and permissions, model-level hardening, output validation, monitoring, and a tested response plan. Each layer assumes that the previous one may fail.
mls-u7-concept-11.example: An agent reads customer email and can issue refunds.
exampleSteps: Content is marked as untrusted, and refund amounts are validated in code.
Refunds above a limit need human approval and are monitored.
If the model is fooled, the damage stays bounded.
mls-u7-concept-11.takeaway: Design so that a single failure stays small.

mls-u1-q01.title: The ML attack surface
mls-u1-q01.statement: A team audits its fraud model’s code and accuracy, but nobody reviews the third-party feed that supplies labels for retraining. Which stage has been left out?

options.a: Output handling in the client
options.b: Data collection and labelling
options.c: Weight storage and loading

mls-u1-q01.hint: Ask where the unreviewed feed enters the pipeline.
mls-u1-q01.explanation: The labels arrive before training, so the feed belongs to the data stage. Whoever controls those labels influences every later retrain.
solutionSteps: The labels arrive before training, so the feed belongs to the data stage. Whoever controls those labels influences every later retrain.
Choose B: Data collection and labelling

mls-u1-q02.title: Security goals for models
mls-u1-q02.statement: An attacker queries a recommender until they can tell whether a specific user’s purchase history was used in training. Which goal is violated?

options.a: Integrity of individual predictions
options.b: Availability of the serving API
options.c: Confidentiality of the training data

mls-u1-q02.hint: Nothing about the predictions changed. What did the attacker learn?
mls-u1-q02.explanation: The model still works correctly and stays online. The harm is that private information about a training record has leaked.
solutionSteps: The model still works correctly and stays online. The harm is that private information about a training record has leaked.
Choose C: Confidentiality of the training data

mls-u1-q03.title: Adversaries are not noise
mls-u1-q03.statement: A team reports 99.2% accuracy on a large random test set and concludes that the model is secure against manipulation. What is the flaw?

options.a: The test set is too large to give a stable estimate of accuracy
options.b: Random test data does not contain inputs chosen to defeat the model
options.c: Accuracy cannot be measured for models that are deployed behind an API

mls-u1-q03.hint: Compare how the test inputs were chosen with how an attacker chooses inputs.
mls-u1-q03.explanation: The test measures the expectation over natural data. Security depends on the worst case over inputs an attacker can construct.
solutionSteps: The test measures the expectation over natural data. Security depends on the worst case over inputs an attacker can construct.
Choose B: Random test data does not contain inputs chosen to defeat the model

mls-u1-q04.title: Why ML bugs resist patching
mls-u1-q04.statement: After a reported bypass, a vendor retrains on the exact attack string and declares the issue fixed. What should a reviewer ask first?

options.a: Whether reworded or adapted variants of the attack still succeed
options.b: Whether the retraining job finished within its scheduled window
options.c: Whether the attack string was stored using a reversible encoding

mls-u1-q04.hint: A patch to one input says little about nearby inputs.
mls-u1-q04.explanation: Retraining on one example shows only that the example is handled. The useful question is whether the underlying class of attack still works.
solutionSteps: Retraining on one example shows only that the example is handled. The useful question is whether the underlying class of attack still works.
Choose A: Whether reworded or adapted variants of the attack still succeed

mls-u1-q05.title: Attacker goals
mls-u1-q05.statement: A malware author modifies a file so that the detector labels it specifically as benign. How is this attack best described?

options.a: Targeted, because one particular output is required
options.b: Untargeted, because the file is the only thing that changes
options.c: Neither, because malware detection has only two classes

mls-u1-q05.hint: Does the attacker accept any output, or do they need one in particular?
mls-u1-q05.explanation: Only the benign verdict helps the attacker, so the attacker needs one specific output. With only two classes the two ideas nearly coincide, but the requirement is still a particular label.
solutionSteps: Only the benign verdict helps the attacker, so the attacker needs one specific output. With only two classes the two ideas nearly coincide, but the requirement is still a particular label.
Choose A: Targeted, because one particular output is required

mls-u1-q06.title: Attacker knowledge
mls-u1-q06.statement: A researcher knows that a product uses a particular open model family and has access to similar training data, but has no access to the deployed weights. Which label fits best?

options.a: White-box
options.b: Black-box
options.c: Grey-box

mls-u1-q06.hint: They know more than the API reveals, but do not have the parameters.
mls-u1-q06.explanation: Partial knowledge of model family and data, without weights, is the grey-box setting.
solutionSteps: Partial knowledge of model family and data, without weights, is the grey-box setting.
Choose C: Grey-box

mls-u1-q07.title: Attacker capabilities
mls-u1-q07.statement: A product retrains nightly on user feedback. Which attack class does this design make possible that a frozen model would not allow?

options.a: Poisoning through submitted feedback
options.b: Evasion using crafted inputs at inference
options.c: Model extraction by repeated querying

mls-u1-q07.hint: Which capability does the retraining pipeline hand to users?
mls-u1-q07.explanation: Evasion and extraction apply to frozen models too. Feeding user data into training is what gives users a training-time capability.
solutionSteps: Evasion and extraction apply to frozen models too. Feeding user data into training is what gives users a training-time capability.
Choose A: Poisoning through submitted feedback

mls-u1-q08.title: Secrecy is not a defence
mls-u1-q08.statement: Which security claim is the most defensible for a model served behind an API?

options.a: It is safe because its architecture has never been published anywhere
options.b: It keeps a useful robust accuracy under attacks that know its full design
options.c: It is safe because its weights are encrypted on the serving machine

mls-u1-q08.hint: Which claim would survive the design becoming public?
mls-u1-q08.explanation: A claim that holds under full knowledge does not depend on secrecy. Hidden designs and encrypted storage do nothing against an attacker who queries the running model.
solutionSteps: A claim that holds under full knowledge does not depend on secrecy. Hidden designs and encrypted storage do nothing against an attacker who queries the running model.
Choose B: It keeps a useful robust accuracy under attacks that know its full design

mls-u1-q09.title: The NIST taxonomy
mls-u1-q09.statement: An attacker alters a small share of a training set so that the finished model misbehaves. Which class does this belong to?

options.a: Evasion
options.b: Privacy
options.c: Poisoning

mls-u1-q09.hint: At what point in the life cycle did the attacker act?
mls-u1-q09.explanation: Interfering with training is poisoning. Evasion happens against a finished model at inference.
solutionSteps: Interfering with training is poisoning. Evasion happens against a finished model at inference.
Choose C: Poisoning

mls-u1-q10.title: MITRE ATLAS
mls-u1-q10.statement: A security team wants to walk through an attack chain step by step and see where its detections have gaps. Which resource suits this best?

options.a: A dataset’s model card
options.b: MITRE ATLAS
options.c: A confusion matrix for the classifier

mls-u1-q10.hint: Which of these describes attacker behaviour across stages?
mls-u1-q10.explanation: ATLAS is organised around adversary tactics and techniques, which suits mapping detections along a chain of attack steps.
solutionSteps: ATLAS is organised around adversary tactics and techniques, which suits mapping detections along a chain of attack steps.
Choose B: MITRE ATLAS

mls-u1-q11.title: The OWASP LLM Top 10
mls-u1-q11.statement: A team passed every item on a Top 10 review and now claims that the application has no remaining AI security risk. Why is the claim too strong?

options.a: The list prioritises common risks and does not enumerate every possible attack
options.b: The list applies only to models that have fewer than ten deployed tools
options.c: The list has been superseded by annual accuracy benchmarks for the model

mls-u1-q11.hint: What is a top ten list designed to do?
mls-u1-q11.explanation: A prioritised list raises the floor. It does not certify that risks outside it, or new variations, are absent.
solutionSteps: A prioritised list raises the floor. It does not certify that risks outside it, or new variations, are absent.
Choose A: The list prioritises common risks and does not enumerate every possible attack

mls-u1-q12.title: Drawing trust boundaries
mls-u1-q12.statement: Which item most clearly crosses a trust boundary into a company’s internal assistant?

options.a: A configuration value set by the deployment team
options.b: A unit test that runs inside the build pipeline
options.c: A web page fetched during a user’s question

mls-u1-q12.hint: Who is able to write the content in each case?
mls-u1-q12.explanation: Anyone on the internet can author a fetched web page, so the content enters the assistant from outside the organisation’s control.
solutionSteps: Anyone on the internet can author a fetched web page, so the content enters the assistant from outside the organisation’s control.
Choose C: A web page fetched during a user’s question

mls-u1-q13.title: Attack success rate
mls-u1-q13.statement: An attack runs against 200 inputs that the model classified correctly. Afterwards, 46 of them are still classified correctly.
mls-u1-q13.prompt: What is the attack success rate, as a decimal?
mls-u1-q13.hint: First work out how many inputs changed.
mls-u1-q13.explanation: The attack succeeded on \(200-46=154\) inputs, so \(\text{ASR}=154/200=0.77\).

mls-u1-q14.title: Clean and robust accuracy
mls-u1-q14.statement: Of 1,000 test images, 940 are classified correctly when clean and 310 remain correct under a stated attack.
mls-u1-q14.prompt: What is the accuracy under this attack, in percent?
mls-u1-q14.hint: Use all 1,000 inputs as the denominator.
mls-u1-q14.explanation: Accuracy under this attack is \(310/1000 = 31\%\). The clean figure of 940 is not part of this calculation.

mls-u1-q15.title: Expected loss
mls-u1-q15.statement: A model theft has a 2% yearly chance and would cost 50,000 euros.
mls-u1-q15.prompt: What is the expected yearly loss, in euros?
mls-u1-q15.hint: Convert 2% to a decimal before multiplying.
mls-u1-q15.explanation: The expected loss is \(0.02 \times 50000 = 1000\) euros per year.

mls-u1-q16.title: Detectors and base rates
mls-u1-q16.statement: Attacks make up 1% of requests. A detector has a true positive rate of 0.90 and a false positive rate of 0.02.
mls-u1-q16.prompt: What is its precision, rounded to two decimals?
mls-u1-q16.hint: Work with 10,000 requests and count the alerts of each kind.
mls-u1-q16.explanation: Out of 10,000 requests, 100 are attacks giving 90 true alerts, and 9,900 are benign giving 198 false alerts. Precision is \(90/288 \approx 0.31\).
solutionSteps: True alerts: \(0.90 \times 100 = 90\).
False alerts: \(0.02 \times 9900 = 198\).
Precision: \(90/(90+198) \approx 0.31\).

mls-u2-q01.title: What an adversarial example is
mls-u2-q01.statement: Which of these is a deliberately crafted adversarial example in the small-perturbation image setting?

options.a: A blurry photo that the classifier happens to get wrong by chance
options.b: A photo deliberately changed imperceptibly so that the classifier’s label flips
options.c: A photo of a new object that was missing from the training classes

mls-u2-q01.hint: Look for both a deliberate change and a preserved meaning.
mls-u2-q01.explanation: Only case B combines a deliberately crafted, small change with an input whose true meaning has not changed.
solutionSteps: Only case B combines a deliberately crafted, small change with an input whose true meaning has not changed.
Choose B: A photo deliberately changed imperceptibly so that the classifier’s label flips

mls-u2-q02.title: Measuring perturbations
mls-u2-q02.hint: Square the entries, add them, then take the square root.

mls-u2-q03.title: Why linear models are enough
mls-u2-q03.statement: A linear model has \(w=(2,-1,3)\). An attacker has an \(L_\infty\) budget of \(\epsilon=0.1\).
mls-u2-q03.prompt: What is the largest increase they can cause in the score?
mls-u2-q03.hint: Add the absolute values of the weights first.

mls-u2-q04.title: Attacks as optimisation
mls-u2-q04.statement: During a white-box evasion attack, which quantity is being updated?

options.a: The input, using the gradient of the loss with respect to it
options.b: The weights, using the gradient of the loss with respect to them
options.c: The labels, using the gradient of the accuracy with respect to them

mls-u2-q04.hint: The model has already been deployed and is not being changed.
mls-u2-q04.explanation: The weights stay fixed. The attacker moves the input in the direction that increases loss.
solutionSteps: The weights stay fixed. The attacker moves the input in the direction that increases loss.
Choose A: The input, using the gradient of the loss with respect to it

mls-u2-q05.title: The fast gradient sign method
mls-u2-q05.prompt: What is the first component of \(x'\)?
mls-u2-q05.explanation: The sign of \(-3\) is \(-1\), so the first component is \(0.5 - 0.1 = 0.4\).

mls-u2-q06.title: Targeted gradient attacks
mls-u2-q06.statement: An attacker wants a specific target class \(t\). Which update moves the input the right way?

options.a: Add \(\epsilon\) times the sign of the gradient of the loss for \(t\)
options.b: Multiply the input by the gradient of the loss for the true label
options.c: Subtract \(\epsilon\) times the sign of the gradient of the loss for \(t\)

mls-u2-q06.hint: The attacker wants the model to treat \(t\) as correct, so that loss should fall.
mls-u2-q06.explanation: Lowering the loss for \(t\) means moving against its gradient, which is the subtraction.
solutionSteps: Lowering the loss for \(t\) means moving against its gradient, which is the subtraction.
Choose C: Subtract \(\epsilon\) times the sign of the gradient of the loss for \(t\)

mls-u2-q07.title: Projected gradient descent
mls-u2-q07.statement: A feature originally equals \(0.50\) and \(\epsilon=0.03\) under \(L_\infty\). A PGD step moves it to \(0.56\).
mls-u2-q07.prompt: What value does the projection give?
mls-u2-q07.hint: Work out the upper limit of the allowed interval.
mls-u2-q07.explanation: The allowed interval is \([0.47, 0.53]\), so \(0.56\) is clipped to \(0.53\).

mls-u2-q08.title: Constraints in the real world
mls-u2-q08.statement: A paper reports strong evasion of a network intrusion detector by editing arbitrary packet fields. Why might the result overstate the real risk?

options.a: Network models cannot be attacked with any gradient-based method
options.b: Some edited packets may no longer be valid or carry out the attack
options.c: Packet data is too low in dimension for perturbations to accumulate

mls-u2-q08.hint: What does the attacker still need the packet to do afterwards?
mls-u2-q08.explanation: An attack only counts if the modified traffic still functions. Unconstrained edits can produce packets that would be dropped or would break the attack.
solutionSteps: An attack only counts if the modified traffic still functions. Unconstrained edits can produce packets that would be dropped or would break the attack.
Choose B: Some edited packets may no longer be valid or carry out the attack

mls-u2-q09.title: Transferability
mls-u2-q09.statement: Why can an attacker craft evasion inputs without any gradient from the target model?

options.a: The target’s gradients are always included in standard API responses
options.b: Examples made on a similar surrogate often transfer to the target
options.c: Adversarial perturbations are random, so any noise works equally well

mls-u2-q09.hint: Where can the attacker get gradients instead?
mls-u2-q09.explanation: The attacker computes gradients on a model they control. Transfer between models carries the effect over to the target.
solutionSteps: The attacker computes gradients on a model they control. Transfer between models carries the effect over to the target.
Choose B: Examples made on a similar surrogate often transfer to the target

mls-u2-q10.title: Estimating gradients with scores
mls-u2-q10.prompt: What is the estimated partial derivative?
solutionSteps: Difference: \(0.04\). Denominator: \(0.02\).

mls-u2-q11.title: The query budget
